name: Virginia Mercury
title: Commentary: Are sales taxes the fairest way to fund improved schools? 47 localities are asking voters to decide.
text:
A view from outside the newly renovated Gloucester County High School, which opened last September. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Amid lingering inflation from high fuel prices, 47 Virginia localities are about to ask their residents to vote on Tuesday for a ballot question that will make every retail purchase they make near their homes costlier.
Interesting timing to say the least. But that doesn’t make it wrong.
If voters approve the proposed tax increases, which are capped at 1%, their proceeds would by law be directed toward capital improvements for public schools in those localities. That’s a worthy purpose, ranking right up there with public safety and healthcare.
Yet the decision is not easy. Voters are being asked to weigh their current financial situations against their children’s futures. There are valid points on either side of this argument that warrant respect.
Still, it’s hard not to feel it’s a shame that it’s come to this.
Virginia localities weigh 1% sales tax for school construction as voters decide on expansion

The sales tax is the most regressive form of taxation there is, burdening most those who have the least. 
The person who works all day then moonlights as a rideshare driver to cover rent, grocery and utility bills with no capacity to save anything pays as much tax on a new refrigerator as a Fortune 500 CEO with a summer house on Martha’s Vineyard and a fleet of Teslas.
It’s a shame because as a commonwealth, our state leaders have preened and posed and positioned themselves as champions of making our schools — in affluent communities and poor ones — safe, modern and excellent, turning out graduates who can hold their own anywhere. You know, the literal definition of a “commonwealth.”
But in the end, the full measure of K-12 educational excellence was tossed back into the laps of Virginia’s 133 localities. 
Because Virginia is a Dillon Rule state — meaning local governments are strictly limited in the tax rates they can raise without legislative approval — the General Assembly empowered the 95 counties and 38 independent cities to ask their voters if they will shoulder a sales tax boost. Thirty-five percent of those localities are doing that in this election.
State approval didn’t happen through the more transparent regular legislative process. A stand-alone bill that would have authorized the extra penny of tax on every dollar’s worth of retail spending passed the House of Delegates this year, but the Senate carried it over to the 2027 session.
The authorization was buried in small type and dense legislative jargon on page 723 of the 887-page state budget enacted on June 29, one day ahead of the deadline for averting a state government shutdown.
Eight Virginia localities — Charlotte, Gloucester, Halifax, Henry, Northampton, Patrick and Pittsylvania counties and the city of Danville — got state permission to ask their voters to approve the sales tax increase before it was extended to all localities this year.
As the Mercury’s Nathaniel Cline explained in his reporting on Oct. 5, those eight localities have generated a combined $119 million through those higher taxes since 2019, but results are mixed and satisfaction is not universal.
In Halifax, the first locality to receive authorization, students enjoy a new high school and remodeled elementary and middle schools that wouldn’t have been affordable without the $20.8 million the county has taken in over the past five years.
Danville took in nearly $31 million from 2023 through last year, giving the city ample bonding authority for impressive upgrades to its facilities.
That’s not bringing much comfort, however, to voters in York County, which would see its combined sales tax rate reach 8% — the highest in Virginia — if the measure passes. Already, York is tied with two of its Peninsula neighbors, James City County and Williamsburg, for the state’s highest rate at 7%.
By no stretch is York County struggling economically. According to the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, its median annual household income is just under $110,000, or about $16,800 greater than the statewide median. 
But that doesn’t translate to York residents gladly paying significantly more in taxes on their purchases than the statewide average of just under 6%.
York County Supervisor G. Stephen Roane Jr. opposed putting the sales tax increase measure on the countywide ballot with so little time to weigh the political and economic consequences against the benefits.
“I thought we needed time to study other options to seek money to provide for school infrastructure projects. I thought we moved too quickly,” he said in an interview.
Particularly, he said, he was concerned about the effect the state’s highest sales tax could have on merchants in his county. Within reason, consumers will travel to save money, and retailers in the cities of Poquoson and Hampton — both sharing York’s eastern boundary — could beckon frugal York shoppers to make the short drive and exploit a tax rate two percentage points lower, especially on big-ticket items.
As incomes go, York’s ranking among the top 10% of the state’s most affluent localities can be quite misleading, Roane noted.
“Affluence is an average across the board, so there are people below that average who are going to struggle,” he said. “You’ve got to be mindful of everybody in the county.”
Virginia as a whole compares favorably to neighboring states when it comes to sales tax burdens. Our average combined state and local rates are about even with those of every adjacent state but Tennessee — a state that proudly eschews an income tax yet forces consumers to pay almost an extra dime on every retail dollar spent except for groceries, which are taxed at a lower rate.
Even with the additional penny of sales taxes for schools, Virginia would still be a bargain compared to Tennessee and wouldn’t make the commonwealth inherently uncompetitive with any other nextdoor state.
The greater question for Virginians heading to the polls, however, is whether this is the most equitable way to invest in our local public schools and, by extension, the commonwealth’s future.
Fortunately, these are the most meaningful and productive questions that we as a commonwealth can and should ask ourselves — at all levels of government. And in the end, there are good answers and better answers, but no wrong ones.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Mixed reactions among disabled Granite Staters on the CFI lawsuit settlement
text:
Kathy Bates, Jim and Pat Piet and Dan Hebert, shown here in their respective homes, each receive services to help them perform the daily activities of life with their disability through New Hampshire's Choices for Independence program. A class action lawsuit over the program's inadequacies was settled earlier this month. (Photos by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)Kathy Bates was elated when she heard that her attorneys and the state of New Hampshire settled a yearslong lawsuit over the Medicaid program that she relies on for care.
Husband and wife duo Jim and Pat Piet are more skeptical and fear that this settlement alone won’t fix the lackluster program without harming other programs.
Dan Hebert, on the other hand, is cautiously optimistic. He sees the potential for big upside, but he also sees pitfalls.
 
Proposed Class Action Settlement For Fitzmorris v DHHS 

Bates, Piet and Hebert are all participants in New Hampshire’s Choices for Independence, a state-run Medicaid program that provides in-home care to people with disabilities and older adults. The goal of the program is to allow them to stay in their own home by hiring caregivers and other supports to avoid a nursing home, something that even the state acknowledges would cost roughly three times as much money.
After years of severe underinvestment in the program, a coalition of nonprofits focused on disability and elderly rights sued the state, arguing that by not properly funding the program the state was at risk of illegally institutionalizing people with disabilities. The case, which lasted almost six years and became a class action lawsuit, was set to go to trial next month before both sides came to an agreement to settle the case earlier this month.
The settlement still must be approved by federal Judge Paul Barbadoro, but class members like Bates, Piet and Hebert have all had a chance to review the settlement, which has major implications on their daily lives.
Elation
Bates is a named plaintiff in the suit. That means she’s been involved in the case since its earliest days and was a representative for the whole class.
“I’m really glad we got here,” she said, before joking, “I probably would’ve said no if I realized it would’ve taken this long.”
Bates, who lives in Somersworth, has cerebral palsy. In 2021, she and three other CFI participants represented by the AARP Foundation, the Disability Rights Center of New Hampshire, New Hampshire Legal Assistance and Nixon Peabody sued the state over the program. Soon after, the case became a class action and grew to encompass the thousands of New Hampshire residents in the CFI program. Bates said she’s relieved the case, which was time-consuming and draining, is over.
Kathy Bates poses for a photo in her Somersworth home on March 25, 2025. Bates said having aides help her with everyday tasks allows her to do fulfilling advocacy work. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
“It feels like it was a part-time job,” she said.  
Core to the plaintiffs’ arguments was that CFI participants weren’t getting the services the state had approved them for. Because of underfunding, CFI participants have long reported, wages were so low that hiring caregivers is near impossible. Vacancies mean shifts go unworked and CFI participants don’t get the help they need to do basic activities of living like getting out of bed, dressing themselves, showering, cooking meals and cleaning. This, their attorneys argued, was putting CFI participants at risk of being put in an institution, a violation of their rights under the 1990 Americans with Disabilities Act and the 1973 Rehabilitation Act. To settle the lawsuit and avert a trial, the state agreed to take a series of steps aimed at solving the issue:

The Department of Health and Human Services agreed to hire a third-party consultant to analyze the state’s network of caregivers to determine whether it meets the needs of the participants. Specifically, the consultant must identify the level of service the state approved for participants versus how much they actually received.
DHHS also agreed to ensure every participant has a contingency plan in place should they not receive their approved services and to execute that plan for any participants who received less than 50% of their approved services each month.
Reimbursement rates set by the state determine caregiver salaries. DHHS agreed to perform an analysis on its reimbursement rates.
DHHS also agreed to ask state lawmakers for biennial reimbursement rate increases to match inflation.
DHHS agreed to expand use of “specialized rates” given to participants who struggle to hire aides.
DHHS agreed to create an online portal and directory of caregivers.
Finally, DHHS agreed to expand its existing grievance system to allow complaints about missed services.
Twice a year, DHHS would be required to create a report outlining its compliance with the agreement.

Bates said the part she’s most excited for is the registry of caregivers. She’s long complained about how challenging it is to hire aides. Bate hires them herself and the caregivers are paid by a third party agency using state funds. She currently uses Craig’s List ads and staffing agencies to find caregivers but is excited to have a new tool she hopes will be more effective. Most of all she’s excited about what it means for the people that help her get out of bed in the morning, people she’s really grateful for.
She hopes “it’ll make the profession of caregiving and the people who do this work” more respected. She explained that lots of her caregivers are single mothers trying to support their own families in addition to supporting her.
“If they make more money in the profession, it becomes a real career option,” she said. “It’ll make life easier for them.”
The New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services, photographed here on Oct. 19, 2026, operates Medicaid in New Hampshire, which encompasses several different programs aimed at supporting people with disabilities in addition to providing low-income Granite Staters with health coverage. The department has agreed to a series of changes to its Choices for Independence Program in exchange for settling a class action lawsuit and . (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
She knows, however, that change will take time.
“I guess I’ll just have to be patient,” she said.
Skepticism
When Pat Vincent-Piet first heard about the settlement, her first question was “like everything, who pays for this again?”
In a class action lawsuit where the plaintiffs’ attorneys represent thousands of people in one suit, complete agreement among class members is very rare.
Pat and Jim Piet live in Concord and both have cerebral palsy. However, cerebral palsy, like many disabilities, has a spectrum of symptoms. Pat does not need the same level of care as Jim, who uses a wheelchair and has caregivers help him perform many of the daily activities of life.
The couple is skeptical. The settlement doesn’t commit the state to spending more money on the program, which would be needed to raise caregiver salaries and ensure all services are provided. It merely instructs DHHS to ask lawmakers to increase funding to match inflation and create reports about the program. The plaintiffs’ attorneys hope the reports demonstrate the dire needs of this program and convince lawmakers to properly fund the program, but DHHS can’t force lawmakers to give it additional funding. And the reports mandated by the settlement do not have to be produced until after the Legislature commences its budget-making process early next year.
“The only way that works is if we take some money from someone else.” Pat said.
Pat is concerned that to fix one Medicaid program, DHHS will have to raid the coffers of another, such as the developmental disability waiver, another Medicaid program that supports people with intellectual and developmental disabilities rather than purely physical ones. She has little confidence the Legislature will give DHHS the funding needed to reform CFI. She pointed to recent cuts to the Medicaid program over the past two years.
Jim and Pat Piet pose for a photo in their Concord home. The couple said that hiring aides to help Jim with everyday tasks in light of his cerebral palsy is “damn near impossible.” (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Medicaid, which is run jointly by states and the federal government, encompasses several programs. In addition to the several that support people with various disabilities, traditional Medicaid offers health coverage to low-income Americans. In 2025, Congress passed a law that KFF estimated will cut $991 billion from Medicaid nationwide. That same year, New Hampshire lawmakers implemented multiple cost-saving measures on the state level. They are set to begin charging premiums to certain traditional Medicaid recipients soon and have decreased the amount of prescription costs the state will cover. Pat argues “all of those things are connected.”
Jim and Pat also questioned whether the state has the staff to create these reports and do the extra work this settlement requires. They said the Medicaid personnel they interact with to get reapproved for services every year and complete other bureaucratic tasks tell them they’re too understaffed to get the work they currently have on their plate done.
“There’s no one to implement these requirements,” Jim said.
Jim and Pat feel they’re luckier than most CFI participants. When they can’t find a caregiver to cover a shift, Pat steps in to help. Single participants don’t have that luxury. Still, Jim wants his wife to be his wife, not his aide. It’s also hindered Pat’s career and her ability to earn a living, pay taxes and contribute to the community.
Cautious optimism
Dan Hebert, who also lives in Concord, had dates set on his calendar for a potential trial and was surprised to learn about the settlement. His takeaway is cautious optimism.
What he likes about the settlement: “a greater push toward transparency” and “what’s hopefully going to be an increase in compensation for the caregivers.”
The class action lawsuit, entitled Fitzmorris v DHHS, was being litigated in the U.S. District Court of New Hampshire, photographed here on Aug. 27, 2025. The case narrowly averted a trial, planned for November, when the parties reached a settlement agreement in early October. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Hebert agrees with the attorneys’ argument that demonstrating the lackluster nature of CFI could push lawmakers to better fund it.
“I counted no less than five reports that are mandated in this,” he said. “And while the department has had this information already, having it in five reports transparently and announced means that everyone sees it upfront and it’s readable. I think that’s important.”
He’s also planning to utilize the grievance system.
“I can’t tell you that it’s going to work,” he said. “I can’t tell you that it’s not going to work. I don’t know, but I do know that the monitoring is going to tell us the truth, and we’re all going to see it.”
Hebert is disappointed the reports won’t be ready before state lawmakers begin budget deliberations as this likely pushes back any real fiscal solution to the problems CFI faces until 2029, the following budget year. He wishes this could be solved sooner.
Dan Hebert, photographed here in his Concord home on Nov. 3, 2025, is one of the CFI participants involved in a lawsuit against the state. He’s hopeful the settlement will be enough to fix the lackluster program. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Overall, he said he’s happy the settlement was struck.
“I think that the attorneys that we have negotiated this settlement to try to do the best that they could,” he said. “And if this is what we’re gonna try, I’m optimistic.”
The Disability Rights Centers, one of the organizations litigating the case, is holding two webinars to inform CFI participants about the settlement on Nov. 17 at 10 a.m and Nov. 30 at 6 p.m. More details are available online at https://cfi.drcnh.org.
Any class member that objects to the settlement can have their voice heard in court on Jan. 21 at the U.S. District Court in Concord. They can also mail in their written complaints by Dec. 7 with the U.S. District Court at 55 Pleasant St. in Concord, NH (ZIP code 03301). Barbadoro, the judge, will decide whether to approve the settlement soon after.
Meanwhile, Hebert still relies on family and friends to help him out because he can’t find enough professional caregivers willing to work for the rates CFI offers.
“My world hasn’t changed today,” Hebert said. “But I’m hoping that it will.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Can Ron DeSantis push Amendment 3 over the top?
text:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis speaking the USF Health Morsani Center for Advanced Healthcare in Tampa on June 25, 2025. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Ron DeSantis was in Crystal River Wednesday, ostensibly to announce that his administration was providing an additional $100 million to restore and protect Florida’s water resources across 45 projects.
However, he spent nearly half of his press conference making the case once again for Amendment 3, the proposal on the statewide ballot that would cut property taxes for Florida homeowners.
With six days to go before Election Day, polls indicate the proposal might be in danger of failing.
A St. Pete Polls survey released Wednesday shows the measure with 44% support, with 39% opposed and 17% unsure. A University of North Florida poll released last week found Amendment 3 getting 50% support. Both would fall far short of the 60% threshold required for passage.
Although the governor has been the main driving force for well over a year-and-a-half in placing the property tax cut proposal before the voters, he initially declined to campaign for it after the Republican-controlled Legislature in June enacted changes to his original language.
He has since reversed that stance and has been actively supporting it, although not in any campaign ads. On Monday, he held a roundtable discussion with U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody and Department of Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson to extoll the proposal’s virtues and praised it again Wednesday as his press conference aired on the Florida Channel.
A variety of organizations have strongly opposed the measure, fearing it would significantly reduce tax revenues for local governments, forcing them to make serious budget cuts. State economists have estimated Amendment 3 would reduce revenue by $5 billion in its first year and as much as $12 billion annually when fully implemented.
The governor made the case in Crystal River that local governments can afford to take a financial haircut, noting they took in $32 billion in property tax revenues in 2019 and now receive $62 billion, well above what he says the pace of inflation and population growth would justify.
“My question is for those who say that we won’t have any services if Amendment 3 passes, did we not have services in 2019?” DeSantis asked. “So, don’t tell me we can’t give our homesteaders a relief. We can do it. One hundred percent.”
Law enforcement agencies such as the Florida Police Chiefs Association, have come out against the measure. In Jacksonville Wednesday, Jennifer “Cookie” Pritt, executive director of the organization, said during a press conference, “Before you vote, ask yourself one question: Where will the money for your local police come from? If no one can give you a straight answer, that tells you what you need to know about Amendment 3.”
DeSantis insisted again that if Amendment 3 passes, he would work with the Legislature to create a fund for fiscally constrained and other “bedroom” communities in places like the Tampa Bay area where they could apply for grants if they need more revenue for “critical needs” — to hire more police officers, for example.
The Legislature killed a provision of the governor’s original proposal that would have created a state trust fund to help local governments cover revenue shortfalls. There is no guarantee lawmakers would agree to do that in the approximately two months DeSantis has left in office.
The governor expressed concern that the Republican turnout hasn’t “been as strong as we would like to see” in vote-by-mail and early voting numbers that have come in. More than 3.7 million Floridians have voted so far, according to the University of Florida Election Lab, with registered Republicans holding a 1.2% lead over registered Democrats, 40.2%-39% (independent and third party registered voters amount to 21% of the state’s vote total to date).
The Republican Party of Florida has endorsed Amendment 3, while the Florida Democratic Party has opposes the measure.
Campaign spending has been heavily titled towards the pro-Amendment 3 forces. A political committee formed by the Florida Realtors to support it has raised more than $21.5 million, according to state election records.  The two political committees opposing Amendment 3, Floridians for Shared Prosperity and Vote No on 3 Florida, have raised a combined $1.3 million.
“I think that we need to do a better job of early voting,” DeSantis said. “Republicans have some work to do, and you guys just got to get out there and vote and then let the people’s will carry the day.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Lack of major property tax relief in Kansas prompts fingerpointing in governor’s race
text:
Democrat Cindy Holscher and Republican Ty Masterson appear at the Sept. 12, 2026, debate at the Kansas State Fair. The two rivals for governor agree on the need to reduce property taxes for homeowners but clash on the details. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson shared with television viewers Jan. 12, 2021, a vision for how Republicans could deal with runaway property taxes.
In the GOP reply to Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly’s State of the State speech, Masterson promised GOP lawmakers would address the burden of $5.4 billion in property taxes collected statewide at that time. It wasn’t an unimaginable political feat given Masterson’s authority over the GOP supermajority in the Senate and House Speaker Dan Hawkins’ control of the two-thirds Republican majority in the House.
It was a politically astute pledge, because polling consistently affirmed property tax applied to homeowners was the most hated, relative to sales and income taxes.
“We must work to enact meaningful property tax reform to allow seniors and families to stay in their homes,” Masterson vowed.
Senate President Ty Masterson, the 2026 Republican nominee for governor, promises in a 2021 video message to make property tax reform a top legislative priority. (Kansas Reflector screen capture of Kansas Legislature video)
The Legislature spent the next five years nibbling on the edge of reform, but annual statewide revenue from property taxes ballooned to $6.6 billion by 2025. Legislators continued to hear from folks outraged by double-digit escalation of property valuations that triggered tax increases even when mill levies remained flat.
Sen. Cindy Holscher, the Democratic Party’s nominee for governor, said Masterson and Hawkins failed to leverage their Republican supermajorities to grapple with property taxes in the manner they did to slash state income taxes and trim the state’s sales tax on groceries. In the 2026 legislative session, the House and Senate ran into gridlock as they took turns voting down competing GOP property tax bills.
“Ty Masterson has had years as Senate president, with a Republican supermajority behind him, and time and again he has repeatedly failed to deliver the property tax relief Kansans need,” Holscher said. “He said, ‘We can do whatever we want because we’re in charge.’ He either doesn’t want to do this or doesn’t know how.”
Masterson, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, joined the outcry. He said he was disappointed obstinate Democrats and “phony Republicans” stood in the way of efforts to limit the ability of school, city and county officials to pile up property tax revenue.
“The truth of why your taxes are so high … people like Cindy have not met one of your tax dollars she didn’t want to spend two of. You have to put constraints on the local government,” Masterson said. “I want to make your life more affordable and property taxes is a big part of that.”
In 1997, residential property owners in Kansas accounted for 38% of property tax revenue, while commercial property owners picked up 62%. The accumulation of tax exemptions for businesses reversed the math. By 2024, residential owners paid 57% of the property tax bill in Kansas and commercial property owners in the state covered 43%.
 
The track record
The Legislature during the past five years considered dozens of ideas for modifying the property tax landscape, but momentum for reform was tempered by the reality that local government received the majority of its funding from property tax. Cities and counties objected to the Legislature wading into their funding stream.
In 2021, the Legislature approved a “truth in taxation” law preventing cities, counties or townships from raising property tax revenue above the previous year’s inflation-adjusted total without mailing advance notice to taxpayers and conducting public hearings before voting on property tax changes.
State lawmakers in 2022 agreed to provide property tax reimbursements to retail business owners subjected to shutdown orders during the COVID-19 pandemic. Attempts by the Legislature to implement vehicle property tax relief prompted vetoes by Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly. Legislators did raise the residential exemption on property taxes to fund K-12 public schools from $20,000 to $40,000. That saved the average homeowner about $46 per year. Meanwhile, the Legislature approved property tax exemptions for telecommunications equipment.
In 2023, lawmakers debated, but failed to pass, an amendment to the Kansas Constitution to cap growth in property valuations that were the cause of higher tax bills for many homeowners.
In 2024, Kelly signed a measure raising the residential property tax exemption to $75,000 when calculating the 20-mill levy for aid to K-12 public schools. The Legislature’s focus that year was on cutting state income taxes. During a special session, the Legislature and governor agreed to a $1.2 billion, three-year reduction.
The Legislature voted in 2025 to eliminate 1.5 mills of state property tax levies relied on to finance state building construction projects. But that $80 million annual reduction in state property tax collections did nothing to change the reality that local governments continued to depend on property taxes for the vast majority of operating revenue. Kansas did adopt a property tax exemption in 2025 for off-road vehicles, boats and trailers.
In 2026, the House and Senate clashed for months without finding consensus on a sweeping property tax fix.
With Masterson’s blessing, the Senate tried to bulldoze through the legislative process an amendment to the Kansas Constitution limiting increases in annual assessment of property values to 3%. The House declined to endorse that approach. Instead, the House sought to prevent local units of government from increasing revenue from property taxes by more than 3% annually. Amid that debate, proposals calling for phasing out the property tax and replacing that revenue with a higher sales tax floundered.
Kelly vetoed a bill in the 2026 session that would have capped city and county spending increases at 3% or the rate of inflation and would have authorized Kansans to file signature petitions to block local property tax increases above that threshold. The governor dismissed the measure as evidence of the legislative leadership’s “false promise” of meaningful property tax reform.
Instead, she encouraged the Legislature to double to $150,000 the portion of a home’s value not subject to property taxes for schools. She recommended creation of a $60 million state fund to reward cities or counties that held budget increases to less than 3%.
 
Sen. Cindy Holscher says many of the Republicans’ ideas for property tax cuts amount to “gimmicks.” (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)
Plans for change
Masterson, who has said during the governor’s race that property tax reform was a top priority, offered voters a “Homeowners Bill of Rights” that would guide the Republican if he were elected governor Nov. 3.
The blueprint would be anchored by a constitutional amendment to cap at 3% annual growth in the valuation of taxable property. In the alternative, the amendment would enable the Legislature to impose a limit on property tax rates. Constitutional amendments require consent from two-thirds of the House and Senate before placed on a statewide ballot.
“I have a neighbor. He’s spending more than double the property tax alone than he had been for his entire mortgage, interest, insurance taxes combined,” Masterson said. “At the same time, that’s putting such a load on our young people to afford housing, and homeownership is the underpinning of the middle class of any country. Our first-time average homeowner is now close to 40, and that’s just not acceptable.”
Masterson, who has represented Andover in the Legislature for 20 years, said he wanted local taxing jurisdictions to secure direct voter consent for “unreasonable” budget increases linked to property tax revenue. He would freeze or reduce property taxes for senior citizens and work toward inhibiting Kansans from being “taxed out” of a home, farm or business.
Holscher, an Overland Park resident elected to the Legislature in 2016, said much of the GOP’s strategy for property tax reform amount to “gimmicks” or concepts designed to financially starve local governments responsible for delivering essential public services.
“They squeeze the balloon, they shuffle the responsibility somewhere else, and it makes it harder for our local levels to raise the revenue they need for their critical services,” she said.
Holscher recommended the Legislature provide funding to fully meet its obligation to finance special education programs in K-12 public schools. When the state avoided its responsibility to students, she said, local school boards were forced to dip deeper into property tax revenue to cover program costs.
“Special education hasn’t been fully funded since 2011,” she said. “We’re federally mandated to fund it. When we don’t do that, that burden gets shifted to the local level.”
The Democratic senator said Kansas ought to lower the taxed percentage of home values from 11.5% to 9%, which would deliver property tax relief to homeowners across all income levels. In addition, Holscher recommended restraining the issuance of tax breaks to wealthy business owners. She also support specific property tax exemptions for seniors and disabled veterans.

title: Commentary: A tale of a law, a lawsuit and many missed opportunities for Kentucky children
text:
The Kentucky Court of Appeals in Frankfort, Kentucky, on Oct. 23, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)At 2:30 Saturday morning, I woke up troubled by the October 23 hearing in the Kentucky Court of Appeals that I had attended.
One thought kept returning: We shouldn’t have been in that courtroom at all.
I had listened as attorneys debated subpoenas, funding, the State Auditor’s authority and whether the dispute was moot. How had a kinship care law intended to protect vulnerable children brought us to this point?
My thoughts returned to a conversation with a grandmother in 2019.
When her grandson was removed from his home, she took him in. She signed paperwork without fully understanding how that decision could affect financial assistance for his care.
She later realized she had potentially waived access to thousands of dollars of assistance. 
I shared her concerns with a senior Cabinet for Health and Family Services official, who acknowledged communication could improve, but maintained the process was legal.
In my view, communication fell short. And something can be legal and still need to change.
That experience helped lead to Senate Bill (SB) 151, unanimously passed by Kentucky’s General Assembly in 2024 and signed by Governor Andy Beshear.
The law established a 120-day window for relatives and fictive kin to understand their options and pursue approval as kinship foster parents. It allowed caregivers experiencing qualifying events to seek reconsideration for foster care approval—potentially keeping children in the same home with support.
It also strengthened opportunities for children to identify relatives or trusted adults they wanted considered for placement.
Then implementation stalled.
The administration cited Fletcher v. Commonwealth, a Kentucky Supreme Court decision concerning legislative appropriations, to justify waiting for additional funding.
CHFS initially estimated implementation at $20 million, later revising that figure to $14.6 million annually. Both estimates relied entirely on state General Fund dollars, despite SB 151’s direction to maximize available federal funding.
I believed Kentucky had other funding options and that portions of the law could have moved forward while financial questions were resolved.
Instead, families waited.
That’s why I asked State Auditor Allison Ball in 2024 to independently examine the funding assumptions behind the delay.
What followed was a legal battle over the Auditor’s authority to obtain information.
Ball sued Governor Beshear and CHFS. The Cabinet maintained it had cooperated with her investigation; Ball argued she lacked information necessary to complete it.
Franklin Circuit Court Judge Thomas Wingate dismissed the lawsuit as premature, citing, in part, the Auditor’s failure to use subpoenas.
On appeal, Ball argued that routinely requiring subpoenas could undermine independent oversight. She cited KRS 43.080, requiring agencies to permit access to records upon the Auditor’s request.
After nearly 30 years in government, I understand what may feel like burdensome information requests. But genuine cooperation means providing what you can and establishing reasonable timelines—avoiding the appearance of a standoff.
If agencies decide what information is sufficient for an independent audit, how independent is that oversight?
Ball warned that without meaningful access to information, her office could become an “empty shell.”  There are implications far beyond SB 151.
In July 2026, CHFS began implementing SB 151 after the General Assembly appropriated $12 million over two years.
The Cabinet now argues that implementation makes the appeal moot.
Really? Moot to whom?
Beginning implementation two years later doesn’t answer whether the original funding estimates were accurate, whether federal funding opportunities and alternative approaches were adequately explored, or whether portions of the law could have been implemented sooner.  
Nor does it restore opportunities lost by families in 2024 and 2025.  
These are questions, not accusations, but answers matter—especially when the full implementation of a law intended to protect vulnerable children was delayed for two years.
In March 2026, a proposed administrative regulation was found deficient following legislative review. I testified, raising concerns about the approach and absence of federal funding.
Then HB 500, the 2026 budget legislation, incorporated language from the proposed regulation, and CHFS proceeded through internal policy.
Questions remain about whether that approach fulfills SB 151’s intent and whether state funding is sustainable. To my knowledge, there is still no approved implementing regulation. I continue working with legislators, CHFS and the Auditor’s office to seek answers.
Meanwhile, children still need their voices heard.
Days before the appeal, I advocated for a teenage foster youth who was in three homes in five days. Although his social worker reportedly had arranged his latest placement days earlier, I was told he learned about the last move when transportation arrived after football practice to take him there. 
SB 151 was intended to strengthen children’s voices in placement decisions.
Was that promise moot to him?
We cannot always change what brings children into the child welfare system. But we can change how government responds.
And that brings me back to the courtroom.
There I sat, a kinship caregiver and advocate, watching State Auditor Allison Ball herself stand at the podium, defending her authority to obtain information.
Our fight began with children and families who deserved better. But it had grown beyond SB 151. The independence of an office responsible for government oversight was now at stake.
The court will decide the legal questions. But the consequences of government decisions don’t disappear when a lawsuit ends.
We don’t need empty shells. We need laws that deliver on all their promises and independent oversight to ensure accountability.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia lawmakers approve plan to advance new K-12 school funding formula
text:
A cup of pencils sit on top of a classroom desk in a Virginia school. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)A state legislative subcommittee on Monday approved a plan to hire an expert to study a new school funding formula for Virginia, with up to 24 months to complete the work.
The decision continues lawmakers’ work to update the state’s 52-year-old funding formula, which determines the Standards of Quality, or funding level for public schools. A December 2023 study showed that Virginia local governments spend far more on K-12 education than the state, underscoring the need for a clearer approach.
Virginia Dept. of Ed projects K-12 schools will need $1.2 billion over next two years

Researchers from the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, which studied the formula, said lawmakers could partially replace the SOQ formula by using student-based calculations for special education and English learner funding. Another option would be to fully replace the entire staffing-based formula with a new student-based formula, researchers said.
Sen. Mamie Locke, D-Hampton, who was re-elected chair of the Joint Subcommittee to Study Elementary and Secondary Education Funding on Monday, said that although the group has 24 months, it would be “optimal” to complete the work when Gov. Abigail Spanberger presents her biennium budget requests in December 2027.
“I don’t think it’s going to take us 24 months to get this work done, and that would be better and in the best interest of our school districts and our kids if we can move this as quickly as possible,” Locke said.
The scope of work requires the consultant to give lawmakers a data-driven tool to evaluate alternative K–12 funding formulas and understand their fiscal and distributional impacts before implementing changes.
Holly Coy, chief of staff for the Virginia Department of Education, said that once the agency finalizes the draft Request for Proposal, or formal service request, it will publish the proposal and accept bids for 30 days. 
The agency expects to select a consultant and begin work during the upcoming General Assembly session in January.
Coy said lawmakers will have an opportunity after the session to provide further input to the consultant on the policy factors that will be built into the funding model. 
Factors include base funding per student, extra weights for student needs, class sizes, operating costs, transition provisions, and the Local Composite Index, which determines what each locality can pay for its schools.
Virginia has increased ongoing K–12 education funding by just over $4 billion, or 50%, from fiscal year 2023 to fiscal year 2028, according to a staff report for the subcommittee, highlighted by $1.5 billion in teacher salaries, plus $375.4 million in one-time educator bonuses.
Other investments include $273.2 million in additional funding for at-risk students, $537.5 million in additional funding for school support staff, $126.8 million to establish and expand dedicated funding for special education, and $106.9 million for additional English language learner teachers and reading specialists positions.
The state has also contributed to additional funding for school construction, early childhood education, and updates to school funding calculations.
Del. Cia Price, D-Newport News, a committee member, expressed support for moving the matter forward without further delay.
“I think this is overdue, and so anything that we can do one time thoughtfully and expeditiously… I think just to put on the record our desire for this to go aggressively, thoughtfully, quickly,” she said.
